screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow is how your program decides what to do next and when to repeat tasks. In iOS apps you will use conditionals to branch behavior based on user input or app state, and loops to process collections or retry actions until a condition changes. This lesson introduces the practical tools you will use: the if, else if, else chain; comparison and logical operators for building conditions; the expressive switch statement for many discrete values; for-in loops for sequences and ranges; while and repeat-while for condition-driven repetition; and break and continue for finer loop control. You will see concrete code examples that match everyday tasks, like showing messages for different ages, handling HTTP status codes with switches, and counting down with loops. I will point out common mistakes such as infinite loops and incorrect operator combinations, and show quick checks you can add to avoid them. By the end you will be able to pick the right control structure for a scenario, write safe loops that terminate, and read others' code faster. Think about a simple app flow you use often — how would you express a user choice and a repeated check in code?

screens.title: If, Else If, and Else
screens.narratorSegment: An if statement evaluates a boolean expression and only runs its block when that expression is true. If you need alternative behavior when the first expression is false, you add an else if to check another expression, and optionally a final else block that runs if none of the previous conditions match. This pattern reads top to bottom: the first true condition wins. A concrete example is displaying different messages by age: check if someone is under thirteen, then under eighteen, then otherwise label them an adult. A common misconception is assuming every condition will be evaluated; once an earlier condition is true, later else if checks are skipped. That matters when later checks include side effects or expensive computations. Another pitfall is mixing up assignment and equality in other languages — in Swift you use equals only for comparison, and assignment cannot appear where a boolean is expected. When writing if-chains, prefer clear, boolean-named expressions such as isLoggedIn or hasID so the code reads like a sentence. As a quick practice, implement a three-branch age check in a playground and run test values at the boundaries to confirm each branch executes as expected. What boundary case will you test first?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › If / Else If / Else
If, Else If, Else
Use sequential checks when conditions are related or mutually exclusive.
Key points:
  • Each condition is a boolean expression using comparison or logical operators.
  • Evaluation stops at the first true branch; later branches are not checked.
  • Use clear names for boolean expressions to make intent obvious.
Concrete example
Age-based messaging: test values around 12, 17, and 18 to confirm branches.
Code walkthrough
// Example of if, else if, else let temperature = 22 if temperature < 0 { print("It's freezing outside!") } else if temperature < 10 { print("It's quite cold.") } else if temperature < 25 { print("It's a pleasant day.") } else { print("It's hot!") }
Common mistake
Writing overlapping ranges without correct order, which causes earlier branches to capture values unexpectedly.
Pro tip
Test boundary values and name booleans, for example isTeenager, to make conditions self-documenting.

screens.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison and logical operators are the ingredients of any condition. Comparison operators like equals, not-equals, less-than, and greater-than let you compare values. Logical operators allow you to combine those comparisons: AND requires both conditions true, OR requires at least one true, and NOT inverts a boolean. A concrete use case is granting access only when a user is both logged in and has an ID; write that as a logical AND. Remember short-circuiting behavior: AND will stop evaluating as soon as one side is false, and OR will stop as soon as one side is true. This saves work but can hide side effects if you put function calls inside expressions. A common misconception is thinking AND and OR have the same priority; use parentheses when expressions get complex to ensure the intended evaluation order. Practice by writing paired checks — for example, require age and subscription status — and then invert the logic with NOT to see the different outcomes. Finally, keep boolean expressions readable by extracting long expressions into well-named constants that describe intent rather than computation. Comparison and Logical Operators means use comparisons to create simple checks, then combine them with logical operators. parentheses clarify order and prevent mistakes.. In practical terms, build precise conditions using comparisons and boolean logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Comparison & Logical Operators
Operators you will use
Comparison operators form atomic checks; logical operators combine them.
Comparison
  • == equals
  • != not equals
  • < > <= >=
Logical
  • && AND (both true)
  • || OR (either true)
  • ! NOT (invert)
Short-circuiting
AND and OR stop evaluating once the result is known. Avoid side-effects in those expressions.
Pro tip
Extract complex checks into named booleans so if (isAuthorized && hasValidSession) reads clearly.
Example: combine checks
// Example of logical operators
let isLoggedIn = true
let hasPremium = false

if isLoggedIn && !hasPremium {
  print("Logged in, but no premium features.")
} else if isLoggedIn || hasPremium {
  print("Either logged in or has premium (or both).")
}
Misconception
Assuming OR checks both sides always; it may short-circuit and skip a later evaluation that has side effects.
Check your understanding
Rewrite a combined expression using intermediate named booleans and confirm behavior stays the same.

screens.title: Switch Statements and Range Matching
screens.narratorSegment: A switch statement compares a single value against multiple cases and runs the block for the first matching case. In Swift, switch is powerful: it can match explicit values, ranges, and even bind parts of a pattern to local variables. An important language rule is exhaustiveness — either your switch lists every possible value for the type, or you include a default case. This prevents unhandled states at runtime. Range matching is handy for grouping numeric values, for example classifying day numbers into weekdays or weekend using a range case. A concrete example is using a status code to print client or server errors via the case 400..<500 and case 500..<600 patterns. A common misconception is treating switch like fallthrough behavior in languages that default to falling through; in Swift cases do not fall through unless you explicitly use the fallthrough keyword, which is rarely necessary. Prefer switch when you have one value and many discrete outcomes; prefer if-chains when checks compare different variables or need complex boolean logic. Try converting a long if-else chain that inspects the same variable to a switch to see improved readability.

keyIdea.title: Switch = clear multi-way match
keyIdea.text: Use switch to organize many possible outcomes from a single value; include default for exhaustiveness when necessary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Switch & Range Matching
When to prefer switch
Switch is ideal when one variable has many possible values or patterns to match.
Benefits:
  • Readable grouping of cases and ranges.
  • Exhaustiveness helps catch unhandled states.
  • Value binding extracts variables directly from matched patterns.
Common pitfall
Expecting implicit fallthrough — Swift does not fall through automatically.
Code example
// Example of switch statement
let dayOfWeek = 3 // 1 = Monday, 7 = Sunday

switch dayOfWeek {
case 1:
  print("It's Monday, start of the week.")
case 2...6:
  print("It's a weekday.")
case 7:
  print("It's Sunday, time to relax!")
default:
  print("Invalid day number.")
}

let statusCode = 404
switch statusCode {
case 200:
  print("Success")
case 400..<500:
  print("Client error: \(statusCode)")
case 500..<600:
  print("Server error: \(statusCode)")
default:
  print("Unknown status")
}
Try this
Convert an if-else chain that checks the same variable into a switch and compare readability and exhaustiveness checks.

screens.title: for-in Loops and Ranges
screens.narratorSegment: The for-in loop is the standard way to iterate over a sequence or range in Swift. It reads simply: for item in sequence {... }. Use closed ranges to include both endpoints, written with three dots, or use a half-open range with two dots and a less-than sign to exclude the upper bound. For example, counting from one to five uses a closed range. You can also iterate over a reversed range if you need descending order. In app development, for-in frequently appears when you process arrays of data to populate lists or compute summaries. A concrete example in a playground is a loading sequence that prints 'Loading item X...' for each item in a 1...5 range. A common mistake is modifying the collection being iterated over; instead, iterate over a copy or collect results into a separate array. Another practical tip is to use underscore as the loop name when you don't need the index value. Also, integrate break into a for-in loop when you want to stop early, such as when an item is found. Practice iterating both forward and reversed ranges and observe how half-open ranges behave on the end value.

keyIdea.title: for-in for sequences
keyIdea.text: Use for-in with closed or half-open ranges to iterate predictable numbers or collections; reverse when needed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › for-in & Ranges
Iterating predictable sequences
Choose closed or half-open ranges depending on whether you include the end value.
Details:
  • Closed range uses three dots: 1...5 includes 5.
  • Half-open range uses <.: 0..<3 excludes 3.
  • Use reversed() for descending order.
Avoid mutation
Do not change a collection while iterating over it; collect results separately instead.
Code example
print("Counting up:")
for number in 1...3 { // Closed range: includes 1, 2, 3
  print(number)
}

print("Counting down:")
for i in (0..<3).reversed() { // Half-open range, then reversed
  print(i)
}
Example use
Iterate items to build table rows or compute totals from an array.
Check
If you don't need the loop variable, use underscore to show intent and avoid unused variable warnings.

screens.title: while vs repeat-while
screens.narratorSegment: While and repeat-while are both used when the number of repetitions is not predetermined and depends on a condition. The key difference is when the condition is checked. A while loop checks the condition before each iteration; if the condition is false initially, the loop body never runs. In contrast, repeat-while checks the condition after each iteration, guaranteeing at least one execution. A practical example is reading user input until they type 'quit': with repeat-while you prompt at least once. A common mistake is assuming both behave the same — that can lead to logic bugs when initialization matters. Another risk is infinite loops: ensure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition false, such as decrementing a counter or updating a flag. Use timeouts or iteration counters during debugging to detect runaway loops in development. When you need guaranteed first execution, use repeat-while; when you want to ensure a precondition holds before any work, prefer while. Try both patterns with a simple countdown and with a simulated user prompt to observe the difference. while vs repeat-while means while checks before running; repeat-while runs once before checking. choose based on whether first execution is required.. In practical terms, condition-checked loops: pre-check and post-check differences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pre-check vs Post-check
keyIdea.text: while checks before running; repeat-while runs once before checking. Choose based on whether first execution is required.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › while vs repeat-while
while loop
Checks condition before each iteration. Use when work should only run if a precondition is true.
var countdown = 3
while countdown > 0 {
  print("T-minus \(countdown)...")
  countdown -= 1
}
print("Liftoff!")
repeat-while loop
Runs once, then checks the condition. Use when you need guaranteed at-least-one execution.
var input: String
repeat {
  print("Enter 'quit' to exit:")
  input = readLine() ?? ""
} while input != "quit"
print("Exited loop.")
Pitfall
Forgetting to change the condition inside the loop causes infinite loops.
Debug tip
Add a debug counter or timeout while testing to detect runaway loops quickly.
Quick exercise
Write both loops for a countdown that starts at zero and observe which one prints at least once.

screens.title: break and continue
screens.narratorSegment: break and continue let you alter the natural flow of loops for practical needs. Use break to immediately exit the current loop when a goal is reached — for example, stop searching once you find a matching item. Use continue when you want to skip the remainder of the current iteration and proceed to the next one — for example, skip processing an out-of-stock product. A concrete scenario is iterating 1 to 5 but stopping early when you reach three; break makes this immediate. A common misuse is overusing break or continue in complex loops, which can make logic harder to follow; prefer early returns or clearer conditions when possible. Another subtlety is that break only exits the innermost loop; nested loops require extra handling. Also, if you rely on loop invariants after a break, ensure you maintain state appropriately. Try the sample loading sequence that breaks at item three, then modify it to continue on item three to see the different outcomes. Reflect on when early exit improves performance versus when it harms readability. break and continue means use break to exit early and continue to skip an iteration; avoid overuse inside deeply nested loops for clarity.. In practical terms, control loop execution when special conditions arise. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fine-grained loop control
keyIdea.text: Use break to exit early and continue to skip an iteration; avoid overuse inside deeply nested loops for clarity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › break & continue
Exit or skip
break leaves the loop entirely; continue moves to the next iteration.
  • break for early exit when a target is found.
  • continue to ignore the rest of the body for this iteration.
  • Only affects the innermost loop; nested loops need additional checks.
Example: loading sequence with break
print("--- Loading Sequence ---")
for itemNumber in 1...5 {
  print("Loading item \(itemNumber)...")
  if itemNumber == 3 {
    print("Item 3 loaded, stopping early.")
    break // Exit the loop
  }
}
Variant: continue
Use continue to skip processing when an item is invalid or out of stock instead of stopping the whole loop.
Readability note
If many breaks and continues appear, consider extracting logic into functions to clarify intent.
Key Takeaway

Use break to stop when done and continue to skip items, but keep loops readable.

screens.title: Playground Example: Conditions and Loops Together
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small playground example that combines conditionals, switch, and loops to show how these tools collaborate. First, we set a userAge and use an if-else chain to print a message for child, teenager, or adult. Then we switch a userRole string to grant access levels; switch makes it easy to read discrete roles. Finally, we run a loading loop using for-in that demonstrates break when a target item is found and continue to skip invalid items. This example shows three common patterns: branching by value, exhaustive matching of states, and iterating until a condition stops the work. While reading the code, watch for short-circuiting in logical expressions and locate where the loop will terminate. A common debugging practice is to run the playground and change the test values — try changing userRole to an unexpected string to see the default switch path, or set a loop bound to a very high number and add a debug counter to prevent long runs. import Foundation let userAge = 25 if userAge < 18 { print("You are eligible for a student discount!") } else if userAge >= 65 { print("You are eligible for a senior discount!") } else { print("No special age-based discount applies.") } let userRole = "admin" // Try changing to "editor", "viewer", or "guest" switch userRole { case "admin": print("Full access granted.") case "editor": print("Can create and modify content.") case "viewer": print("Can view content only.") default: print("Unknown role. Limited access.") } print(" --- Loading Sequence ---") for itemNumber in 1...5 { print("Loading item \(itemNumber)...") if itemNumber == 3 { print("Item 3 loaded, stopping early.") break } }

screens.title: Choosing Between if Chains and switch
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an if-else chain and a switch often comes down to clarity and the kind of checks you are performing. Use if-else chains when conditions involve different variables or complex boolean expressions, for example combining weight and destination when calculating shipping costs. If you are testing one value against many possible discrete states — like user roles or enum cases — a switch is usually clearer and enforces exhaustiveness. Switch also excels at range matching and value binding, letting you extract parts of a value directly in a case. A common misconception is that switch is always faster; performance depends on the compiler and the specific patterns, but switch can improve readability and reduce mistakes by requiring you to handle unexpected values. A practical heuristic: if all branches check the same variable, prefer switch; if not, prefer if-else. Try the assessment scenario: decide whether shipping cost logic should be an if-chain — because it mixes weight and destination — or a switch — because it is testing a single enum of shipping tiers. Use this heuristic as a readability guide when refactoring code.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Tips
screens.narratorSegment: A few practical reminders will make control flow robust in real projects. First, test boundary values for ranges and age-like checks: boundaries are where bugs hide. Finally, prefer switch when matching the same value across many outcomes, and if you convert an if-chain to switch, remember to satisfy exhaustiveness. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Practical Tips
Test boundaries
Always run inputs at the edges of ranges and condition checks to confirm correct branch selection.
No side effects in logic
Keep function calls that change state out of logical expressions because short-circuiting can skip them unexpectedly.

fullNarratorScript:
Control flow is how your program decides what to do next and when to repeat tasks. In iOS apps you will use conditionals to branch behavior based on user input or app state, and loops to process collections or retry actions until a condition changes. This lesson introduces the practical tools you will use: the if, else if, else chain; comparison and logical operators for building conditions; the expressive switch statement for many discrete values; for-in loops for sequences and ranges; while and repeat-while for condition-driven repetition; and break and continue for finer loop control. You will see concrete code examples that match everyday tasks, like showing messages for different ages, handling HTTP status codes with switches, and counting down with loops. I will point out common mistakes such as infinite loops and incorrect operator combinations, and show quick checks you can add to avoid them. By the end you will be able to pick the right control structure for a scenario, write safe loops that terminate, and read others' code faster. Think about a simple app flow you use often — how would you express a user choice and a repeated check in code?

In this set of learning objectives we map what you'll practice to observable skills. First, you'll implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else so your code performs different actions depending on data. A practical example is showing different UI text based on a user's age. Second, we'll work with comparison and logical operators to build compound expressions — for example checking that a user is both logged in and has an ID before granting access. Third, you'll learn to apply the switch statement for many discrete values and ranges, and understand Swift's exhaustiveness requirement. Finally, you'll begin using for-in loops to iterate over sequences and ranges so you can process lists of items. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify in a playground. These objectives are designed to guide practice and code reading, so you become fluent in choosing the right control structure for a task.

This continuation of objectives narrows in on safe and expressive use of control flow. You'll master comparison operators such as equals, not-equals, and inequality operators so you read and write precise conditions. You'll practice logical operators to combine checks, and you will learn the difference between short-circuiting AND and OR so you avoid unexpected evaluations. For switch statements you'll practice range cases and value binding, and you'll learn why Swift demands exhaustive handling or a default case. For loops, you'll practice both for-in and condition-driven loops, and introduce break and continue to alter iteration when a special case appears. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or mini-visual to help you remember when to pick a structure. Finally, we emphasize safe loop termination to prevent infinite loops, and small debugging checks you can add to catch issues quickly while running in a playground or during testing.

An if statement evaluates a boolean expression and only runs its block when that expression is true. If you need alternative behavior when the first expression is false, you add an else if to check another expression, and optionally a final else block that runs if none of the previous conditions match. This pattern reads top to bottom: the first true condition wins. A concrete example is displaying different messages by age: check if someone is under thirteen, then under eighteen, then otherwise label them an adult. A common misconception is assuming every condition will be evaluated; once an earlier condition is true, later else if checks are skipped. That matters when later checks include side effects or expensive computations. Another pitfall is mixing up assignment and equality in other languages — in Swift you use equals only for comparison, and assignment cannot appear where a boolean is expected. When writing if-chains, prefer clear, boolean-named expressions such as isLoggedIn or hasID so the code reads like a sentence. As a quick practice, implement a three-branch age check in a playground and run test values at the boundaries to confirm each branch executes as expected. What boundary case will you test first?

Comparison and logical operators are the ingredients of any condition. Comparison operators like equals, not-equals, less-than, and greater-than let you compare values. Logical operators allow you to combine those comparisons: AND requires both conditions true, OR requires at least one true, and NOT inverts a boolean. A concrete use case is granting access only when a user is both logged in and has an ID; write that as a logical AND. Remember short-circuiting behavior: AND will stop evaluating as soon as one side is false, and OR will stop as soon as one side is true. This saves work but can hide side effects if you put function calls inside expressions. A common misconception is thinking AND and OR have the same priority; use parentheses when expressions get complex to ensure the intended evaluation order. Practice by writing paired checks — for example, require age and subscription status — and then invert the logic with NOT to see the different outcomes. Finally, keep boolean expressions readable by extracting long expressions into well-named constants that describe intent rather than computation. Comparison and Logical Operators means use comparisons to create simple checks, then combine them with logical operators. parentheses clarify order and prevent mistakes.. In practical terms, build precise conditions using comparisons and boolean logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A switch statement compares a single value against multiple cases and runs the block for the first matching case. In Swift, switch is powerful: it can match explicit values, ranges, and even bind parts of a pattern to local variables. An important language rule is exhaustiveness — either your switch lists every possible value for the type, or you include a default case. This prevents unhandled states at runtime. Range matching is handy for grouping numeric values, for example classifying day numbers into weekdays or weekend using a range case. A concrete example is using a status code to print client or server errors via the case 400..<500 and case 500..<600 patterns. A common misconception is treating switch like fallthrough behavior in languages that default to falling through; in Swift cases do not fall through unless you explicitly use the fallthrough keyword, which is rarely necessary. Prefer switch when you have one value and many discrete outcomes; prefer if-chains when checks compare different variables or need complex boolean logic. Try converting a long if-else chain that inspects the same variable to a switch to see improved readability.

The for-in loop is the standard way to iterate over a sequence or range in Swift. It reads simply: for item in sequence {... }. Use closed ranges to include both endpoints, written with three dots, or use a half-open range with two dots and a less-than sign to exclude the upper bound. For example, counting from one to five uses a closed range. You can also iterate over a reversed range if you need descending order. In app development, for-in frequently appears when you process arrays of data to populate lists or compute summaries. A concrete example in a playground is a loading sequence that prints 'Loading item X...' for each item in a 1...5 range. A common mistake is modifying the collection being iterated over; instead, iterate over a copy or collect results into a separate array. Another practical tip is to use underscore as the loop name when you don't need the index value. Also, integrate break into a for-in loop when you want to stop early, such as when an item is found. Practice iterating both forward and reversed ranges and observe how half-open ranges behave on the end value.

While and repeat-while are both used when the number of repetitions is not predetermined and depends on a condition. The key difference is when the condition is checked. A while loop checks the condition before each iteration; if the condition is false initially, the loop body never runs. In contrast, repeat-while checks the condition after each iteration, guaranteeing at least one execution. A practical example is reading user input until they type 'quit': with repeat-while you prompt at least once. A common mistake is assuming both behave the same — that can lead to logic bugs when initialization matters. Another risk is infinite loops: ensure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition false, such as decrementing a counter or updating a flag. Use timeouts or iteration counters during debugging to detect runaway loops in development. When you need guaranteed first execution, use repeat-while; when you want to ensure a precondition holds before any work, prefer while. Try both patterns with a simple countdown and with a simulated user prompt to observe the difference. while vs repeat-while means while checks before running; repeat-while runs once before checking. choose based on whether first execution is required.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

break and continue let you alter the natural flow of loops for practical needs. Use break to immediately exit the current loop when a goal is reached — for example, stop searching once you find a matching item. Use continue when you want to skip the remainder of the current iteration and proceed to the next one — for example, skip processing an out-of-stock product. A concrete scenario is iterating 1 to 5 but stopping early when you reach three; break makes this immediate. A common misuse is overusing break or continue in complex loops, which can make logic harder to follow; prefer early returns or clearer conditions when possible. Another subtlety is that break only exits the innermost loop; nested loops require extra handling. Also, if you rely on loop invariants after a break, ensure you maintain state appropriately. Try the sample loading sequence that breaks at item three, then modify it to continue on item three to see the different outcomes.
